title: A semi-experimental procedure for the estimation of permeability of microfluidic pore network
author: Pradhan, Shaik, et al.

steps.title: Prime system and remove air
steps.instruction: Inject de‑ionized water through the microfluidic chip at approximately 500 μL/min until the flow line and the porous network are completely free of air bubbles.

steps.title: Set test flow rate and record inlet pressure
steps.instruction: Adjust the pump to one of the test flow rates (50, 75, 100, 125, 150, or 175 μL/min). After the flow stabilizes, record at least fifty consecutive injection‑pump pressure readings (P1) with the chip outlet open to atmosphere and calculate their average.

steps.title: Disconnect chip and record pump pressure
steps.instruction: While maintaining the same flow rate, disconnect the microfluidic chip from the inlet tubing. Record another set of at least fifty pump pressure readings (P2) for that flow rate and average them.

steps.title: Calculate chip pressure drop
steps.instruction: For each flow rate compute the pressure drop across the chip: ΔPchip = P1 – P2 (expressed in mbar). Example for 100 μL/min: P1 = 4410 mbar, P2 = 3795 mbar, ΔPchip = 615 mbar.

steps.title: Estimate channel pressure drops
steps.instruction: Calculate the hydraulic resistance of the inlet and outlet rectangular channels using Rh ≈ 12 μ L / [w h³] · (1‑0.63 h/w), where μ = 0.9321 cP (water at 23 °C), L is the channel length, w and h are width and height (width ≫ height; width/height ratios 27, 22, 17). Convert the volumetric flow rate q to m³/s, obtain ΔPinlet = Rh·q, set ΔPoutlet = ΔPinlet (symmetry), and compute ΔPchannels = ΔPinlet + ΔPoutlet = 2·ΔPinlet. For the example, ΔPinlet ≈ 178 mbar, so ΔPchannels = 356 mbar.

steps.title: Determine pore‑network pressure drop
steps.instruction: Subtract the channel pressure drop from the total chip pressure drop: ΔPpore = ΔPchip – ΔPchannels. Convert to atm if required (1 atm = 1013 mbar). Example: ΔPpore = 615 mbar – 356 mbar = 259 mbar = 0.256 atm.

steps.title: Compute absolute permeability
steps.instruction: Apply Darcy’s law: k = (μ·q·L) / (A·ΔPpore). Use q in cm³/s (e.g., 100 μL/min = 0.00167 cm³/s), μ = 0.9321 cP, L = 1 cm, A = 0.002 cm², and ΔPpore in atm. For the example, k = 6.39 Darcy.

steps.title: Repeat for all flow rates and average
steps.instruction: Perform steps 2–7 for each flow rate (50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175 μL/min). Tabulate the resulting permeabilities (e.g., 50 μL/min → 6.477 Darcy, 75 μL/min → 5.891 Darcy, 100 μL/min → 6.391 Darcy, 125 μL/min → 6.451 Darcy, 150 μL/min → 6.401 Darcy, 175 μL/min → 6.75 Darcy). Calculate the mean and standard deviation: k_avg = 6.39 ± 0.28 Darcy.
